Game: Drag the point on the arch and watch where the sloping line crosses the upright line.
How to play: Drag D with a mouse or finger, or focus it and use the arrow keys. Slide A or B to change the arch, tick the boxes to show more, and press Check the claim.
Look for the math

Archimedes found a surprising fact about a semicircle and two touching lines: a third line always cuts a certain upright segment exactly in half. The cut-the-knot page now shows a GeoGebra version, but the Java applet it replaced had the same claim and the same three display switches. The logic test checks the claim at 192 positions of the moving point and four different diameters.

What the picture claims

Let AB be the diameter of a semicircle and let D be any other point on the arc. The tangents at B and D meet at T. Drop DE straight down to the diameter, and let AT cross DE at F. Proposition 2 of the Book of Lemmas says

DF = FE  — that is, F is the midpoint of DE.

In the drawing, the two halves of DE are painted green and gold so you can see them change size together as you drag.

The two tangents have equal lengths

Two tangents drawn from the same point to a circle have the same length, so TB = TD. The angle at D in the triangle ADB is a right angle — this is Thales' theorem, because AB is a diameter. The logic test measures that right angle and the two tangent lengths at every one of its 192 test positions; both claims hold.

Where the extra point H lands

Extend AD until it meets the tangent at B at H. Since AD is at right angles to DB, the angle BDH is right too. So D lies on the circle whose diameter is BH. Because TB = TD, and T lies on the line BH, T is the centre of that circle. Hence HT = TB, exactly as the page's proof says. Tick hint to see that circle and the line through H.

Why F is the halfway point

Both DE and BH are at right angles to AB, so they are parallel. Shrink the whole triangle AHB towards A by any factor λ: H lands on D and B lands on E. The same shrink sends the midpoint T of BH to the midpoint of DE. But the line from A to T is just where that moving midpoint travels, so it meets DE at its midpoint F. Therefore DF = FE for every position of D, not just the one on screen.

The original let D go all the way to A, where the tangents meet far outside any picture. Here the arc stops just short of the ends so that T and the hint circle stay visible; the claim itself holds on the whole open arc.

Try sliding both ends of the diameter inward to make a small arch, then drag D close to an end and watch the two coloured halves grow together.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
